title: Joshua 18:11–28
context: Benjamin’s lot falls between Judah and Joseph. The unit traces the northern, western, southern, and eastern borders and then lists two groups of towns, twelve and fourteen. Many places are known from later history (Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah, Mizpeh, Jerusalem), while the locations of others remain uncertain.

verses.text: The lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up according to their families. The border of their lot went out between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph.
verses.arminianNotes: Benjamin’s lot falls between Judah and Joseph. Arminian readers note that the tribe of Jacob’s youngest son receives a central place, a placement that would shape the tribe’s later history.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s ordering in Benjamin’s location between the two leading tribes. From this tribe would later come Saul, Israel’s first king (1 Samuel 9:1-2), and the apostle Paul (Philippians 3:5).

verses.text: Their border on the north quarter was from the Jordan. The border went up to the side of Jericho on the north, and went up through the hill country westward. It ended at the wilderness of Beth Aven.
verses.arminianNotes: The northern border runs from the Jordan past Jericho and up through the hill country toward the wilderness of Beth Aven. Arminian readers see in the detail a God who gives his people a real and specific place to live.
verses.reformedNotes: Beth Aven appears elsewhere near Ai and Bethel (Joshua 7:2), and Hosea later uses the name for Bethel (Hosea 4:15). Reformed readers note the border without pressing a precise site, since the location is uncertain.

verses.text: The border passed along from there to Luz, to the side of Luz (also called Bethel), southward. The border went down to Ataroth Addar, by the mountain that lies on the south of Beth Horon the lower.
verses.arminianNotes: The border passes Luz, also called Bethel, where Jacob met God in a dream (Genesis 28:19). Arminian readers see the inheritance tied to places of earlier encounter with God, inviting Israel to remember his faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the border passes through places linked to the patriarchs. God’s promise to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:13-15) is now being worked out in the land itself.

verses.text: The border extended, and turned around on the west quarter southward, from the mountain that lies before Beth Horon southward; and ended at Kiriath Baal (also called Kiriath Jearim), a city of the children of Judah. This was the west quarter.
verses.arminianNotes: The western border turns south and ends at Kiriath Baal, also called Kiriath Jearim, a city of Judah. Arminian readers note that tribal borders touched, so neighboring tribes had to cooperate.
verses.reformedNotes: Kiriath Jearim later held the ark for many years (1 Samuel 7:1-2). Reformed readers note how places named in the boundary lists reappear in God’s later dealings with Israel.

verses.text: The south quarter was from the farthest part of Kiriath Jearim. The border went out westward, and went out to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.
verses.arminianNotes: The southern border begins at the farthest part of Kiriath Jearim and runs to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. Arminian readers note the shared border with Judah, also described in 15:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the same landmarks appear in Judah’s border, confirming that the allotments fit together. The exact site of the spring of Nephtoah is uncertain.

verses.text: The border went down to the farthest part of the mountain that lies before the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is in the valley of Rephaim northward. It went down to the valley of Hinnom, to the side of the Jebusite southward, and went down to En Rogel.
verses.arminianNotes: The border runs past the valley of the son of Hinnom and near the Jebusite city. Arminian readers note that this valley later became associated with idolatry and child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31).
verses.reformedNotes: The Hebrew name of the valley of Hinnom stands behind the later word Gehenna. Reformed readers note the sober history of the place, while recognizing that here it is simply a boundary marker.

verses.text: It extended northward, went out at En Shemesh, and went out to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. It went down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.
verses.arminianNotes: The border goes out at En Shemesh and Geliloth toward the stone of Bohan, son of Reuben. Arminian readers note that such landmarks were familiar to the original hearers, even if they are hard to locate now.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the stone of Bohan also appears in Judah’s border (15:6). The exact locations of En Shemesh and Geliloth are uncertain, and the text does not explain the stone’s name.

verses.text: It passed along to the side opposite the Arabah northward, and went down to the Arabah.
verses.arminianNotes: The border passes along opposite the Arabah and goes down to it. Arminian readers note the descent from the hill country to the Jordan valley, a vivid sense of the land’s terrain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boundary tracing the varied geography of Benjamin’s territory, from hills to the rift valley. God’s gift includes land of many kinds.

verses.text: The border passed along to the side of Beth Hoglah northward; and the border ended at the north bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan. This was the south border.
verses.arminianNotes: The southern border ends at the north bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan. Arminian readers note the complete circuit, giving Benjamin a clearly defined inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Beth Hoglah and the Salt Sea mark the southeastern corner. The precision of the boundary reflects God’s care in fulfilling his promise.

verses.text: The Jordan was its border on the east quarter. This was the inheritance of the children of Benjamin, by the borders around it, according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: The Jordan forms the eastern border. Arminian readers see the summary as a reminder that Benjamin’s inheritance was complete and should be received with gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes: The verse closes the border description by naming it the inheritance of Benjamin according to their families. Reformed readers see God’s gift extending to each family within the tribe.

verses.text: Now the cities of the tribe of the children of Benjamin according to their families were Jericho, Beth Hoglah, Emek Keziz,
verses.arminianNotes: Jericho heads the list of Benjamin’s cities, the city whose walls fell at the start of the conquest (Joshua 6). Arminian readers see a reminder of God’s power at the beginning and of his continued provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jericho, under Joshua’s curse against rebuilding (6:26), is still counted in Benjamin’s inheritance, and that 1 Kings 16:34 records the curse’s fulfillment when it was rebuilt.

verses.arminianNotes: Bethel is listed among Benjamin’s cities, a place of patriarchal worship. Arminian readers note that it later became a center of false worship under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:29), a warning about how sacred places can be corrupted.
verses.reformedNotes: Zemaraim later appears as a mountain where Abijah spoke to Jeroboam’s army (2 Chronicles 13:4). Reformed readers note that the list includes places that would figure in later conflicts within Israel.

verses.arminianNotes: Avvim, Parah, and Ophrah follow in the list. Arminian interpreters observe that this Ophrah is generally distinguished from Gideon’s Ophrah of the Abiezrites (Judges 6:11), whose clan appears in 17:2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers acknowledge that little is known of some of these towns. Their inclusion shows that every place, famous or obscure, is part of the inheritance God gives.

verses.text: Chephar Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba; twelve cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Chephar Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba complete the first group of twelve cities. Arminian readers note that Geba later appears in Saul’s battles against the Philistines (1 Samuel 13-14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the summary, twelve cities with their villages, which shows the completeness of the first group and God’s attention to villages as well as towns.

verses.arminianNotes: Gibeon, Ramah, and Beeroth begin the second group. Arminian readers recall that Gibeon and Beeroth were among the Gibeonite cities that made a treaty with Israel (Joshua 9:17), now living within Benjamin’s territory.
verses.reformedNotes: Ramah later became Samuel’s home (1 Samuel 7:17) and is echoed in Jeremiah 31:15, which Matthew 2:18 quotes. Reformed readers see how humble place names become part of the larger story of redemption.

verses.arminianNotes: Mizpeh, Chephirah, and Mozah come next. Mizpeh later became the place where Samuel called Israel to put away foreign gods, fast, and confess their sin (1 Samuel 7:3-6). Arminian readers value that scene as a model of repentance freely offered and graciously received.
verses.reformedNotes: Chephirah was another of the Gibeonite cities (Joshua 9:17). Reformed readers see in this a reminder that God’s people lived alongside those who had sought peace with them.

verses.arminianNotes: Rekem, Irpeel, and Taralah are otherwise little known. Arminian readers note that even obscure towns were real homes for families who received God’s gift and were called to live faithfully there.
verses.reformedNotes: The locations of these towns are uncertain. Reformed readers often hear in such lists the confession of Psalm 16:5-6, that God maintains his people’s lot and that the lines have fallen in pleasant places.

verses.text: Zelah, Eleph, the Jebusite (also called Jerusalem), Gibeath, and Kiriath; fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the children of Benjamin according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Zelah, Eleph, the Jebusite city also called Jerusalem, Gibeath, and Kiriath complete the list. Arminian readers note that Judges 1:21 records Benjamin’s failure to drive out the Jebusites, a theme that echoes 17:12.
verses.reformedNotes: Jerusalem appears here as a Benjamite border city, long before David made it his capital. Reformed readers see God’s future purposes hidden in a simple list; Saul was later buried in Zela (2 Samuel 21:14).
